newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - S.African CPI seen up 0.7 pct in August.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - S.African CPI seen up 0.7 pct in August.

text.p: A strong increase in food prices combined with technical factors should push South African year-on-year consumer price inflation sharply higher in August, economists polled by Reuters said on Friday.

The consensus forecast for the figure, due on Thursday at 0900 GMT, was 7.7 percent from 7.1 percent in July, when consumer inflation rose above seven percent for the first time since August last year.
The range for the year-on-year figure was put at between 7.6 and 7.9 percent, while the month-on-month rate of increase was seen little changed at 0.7 percent from 0.8 percent in July.
Economists said further upward pressure on inflation, which began with a 1.0 percentage point increase in June, would come from a substantial increase in the food component of the index.

Vegetable and fruit prices in particular were expected to have risen sharply following the cold weather experienced in July, while Sanlam economist Pieter Calitz said he also expected meat prices to rise sharply in the month.
A low base figure in August 1995 was also seen contributing as was the feeding through of price pressures due to the rand's plunge since mid-February.
Nick Barnardt, economist at BOE Natwest, said inflation would push higher throughout the next few months, driven by food price pressure and the effects of the currency decline.
"Food inflation will be on an up-trend from now on...also one must allow for the possibility of the rand depreciation to come through," he said.

Rand Merchant Bank treasury economist Julia Roy noted that an unfavourable base effect would probably be very obvious in the food component of the index because of a 1.2 percent month-on-month decline in the food index in August 1995.
Looking ahead, economists expected a year-on-year figure firmly above eight percent in September, rising towards nine percent by year-end.
"We expect a rising trend over the remaining months towards nine percent at year-end," Roy said.
